text:
SpaceX ($SPCX) has asked federal regulators for permission to put up to 1 million solar-powered computing satellites in orbit. After the November 3 midterms, Elon Musk (@elonmusk) offered a fresh reason to pursue the idea. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he wrote on X.

On Earth, SpaceX already had 1.7 gigawatts of computing capacity as of September 30. Adding more means securing electricity, land, water and local approvals. Texas, a major market for new data centers, just elected a governor who campaigned for stronger protections for residents and an end to tax breaks for developers.

Orbit offers an obvious attraction. Satellites could spend much of their time in sunlight, generating electricity without adding demand to a local power grid. SpaceX has discussed initial demonstrations in late 2027, with broader deployment potentially beginning in 2028.

Getting rid of heat is harder. A server on Earth can shed heat into moving air or water. In a vacuum, an orbiting facility has to radiate that heat away through large surfaces that also have to fit on a rocket and deploy reliably.

The million-satellite figure is the upper limit SpaceX requested. Long before it needs that many, the company has to show that a small group of satellites can run useful AI workloads, stay cool and send the results back to customers at a competitive cost.

6. Krafting Darts 📉 −2 (5–3)

Krafting scored 142.34 and lost by 70.28. That is what happens when the opponent reaches 212.62, but the difficult matchup should not obscure the roster issues underneath it.

Brissett scored 3.46, Flowers scored zero, Taylor had 6.7, and Reichard contributed nothing. Hubbard’s 24.9, Michael Wilson’s 26.8 and Tucker Kraft’s 17.3 kept the score respectable. Too many normally important positions failed simultaneously.

The quarterback problem has changed substantially. Arizona named Minshew its starter and Beck its backup, moving Brissett into the emergency third role. Warren then acquired Minshew for $14. Krafting still has Caleb, Nix and Willis, but Brissett can no longer be treated as available weekly production without another NFL depth-chart change.

Nix’s 19.28 sitting on the bench is relevant because quarterback depth only helps when the right players are used. The immediate priority is selecting the healthiest, most secure starting pair rather than assuming the roster’s quantity guarantees a strong result.

Flowers faces a different problem. Huntley is reportedly out for the season, Lamar is headed to IR, and Fagnano will start Thursday. Flowers had zero catches on five targets last week. His talent is unchanged, but the offense creating his opportunities has become much less predictable. 

Wilson’s 26.8 offers a potential answer, though he is playing through two broken ribs. Bourne’s move to IR removes another receiver, potentially increasing Wilson’s importance to Arizona while also leaving him with more defensive attention. That is a combination of opportunity and risk rather than an uncomplicated upgrade.

Evans returning would be especially valuable now, but the Achilles issue still needs to improve enough for him to play. The fantasy trade with yurGirl was supposed to buy reliable veteran production for the playoff push. Until Evans returns, Krafting has paid the pick without receiving the intended lineup stability.

Taylor’s quiet week came in a 42–7 Colts loss with the starters eventually pulled. Indianapolis’s offensive struggles and the Quenton Nelson trade are worth monitoring, but one blowout does not justify abandoning a core player. Hubbard and Kyren give Krafting additional ways to generate points if Taylor’s environment remains difficult.

Against Justin, Krafting’s projected advantage is in the available receiving and flex options. Justin can counter with Bucky, Saquon, Javonte and quarterback depth. Flowers’s new quarterback situation and Wilson’s ribs make that receiver advantage less secure than the names alone suggest.

A loss puts Krafting at 5–4 and Justin at 4–5. With yurGirl holding Krafting’s 2027 first, the consequences extend beyond this year’s standings.

This is the point where a playoff push needs actual lineup improvements, not simply a list of players who might be healthy soon.

text:
Charlie’s vision for Turning Point Action was always bigger than one election. He wanted a permanent, year-round operation with the people, relationships, and resources to compete in every cycle. He knew there would be victories and setbacks because he had experienced both and that’s why he built for both. 

Last night, we saw races Republicans once won handily by double digits come down to the thinnest of margins, and in some cases, flip entirely. Democratic socialist candidates made the cost of gas, groceries, and housing the center of their campaigns. And voters responded at the ballot box. A rising stock market doesn’t mean much when nearly half of Americans don’t have a 401K and just want to put gas in their trucks, put food on the table, and provide a good life for their families. 

But every time socialism has tried it has failed, because socialism concentrates economic power in the hands of the government instead of trusting individuals to build prosperity for themselves and their families. That’s fundamentally at odds with the free enterprise, individual liberty, and opportunity at the heart of the American experiment. We can disagree with the solutions voters were offered while still recognizing why they were looking elsewhere for answers. Exit polls clearly showed that the American people are concerned about the state of the economy and the war in Iran. This isn’t a surprise to us because we’ve heard the same concerns from our students around the country for months and we’ve been concerned about it too. 

The biggest mistake conservatives can make right now would be to allow this moment to become another exercise in finger-pointing, in-fighting, or trying to secure their own political preservation. That does not solve the problems the American people are demanding be solved. 

Turning Point was born out of a moment just like this following the Obama era, which was itself a reaction to the political frustration of the early 2000’s. Our history reminds us that moments of disappointment can actually be moments of renewal and infinite opportunity. 

Americans are not looking for labels and don’t subscribe to unquestioned party loyalty anymore either. They will support the candidates who can both speak to their concerns and deliver on what THEY need and dream about for their families. And those needs are the same as they have always been: an affordable home, safe communities, and the hope that the next generation will inherit a country with more opportunity than the last generation did. That is what the American dream has promised to all of us. 

I miss Charlie so much every single day, but especially on a day like today. He always said that when things are going well, we need to stay humble. And when things aren’t going the way we want, we need to stay positive, keep our faith, and get back to work. 

That’s exactly what we’re doing over at Turning Point today. We are going to listen, study the results, and spend the next two years making the case for how conservative, free market solutions, and a renewed focus on our country’s founding principles can address the problems the American people face. And we’re going to keep building the permanent infrastructure Charlie envisioned, strengthening our relationships in communities across the country, and preparing for 2028 and beyond.

If you woke up feeling discouraged today, there’s more important work to do than ever. Our principles haven’t changed and neither has our mission.

To every staff member, student, volunteer, and ballot chaser who gave their time and energy to this mission this cycle, thank you. I know Charlie would be unbelievably proud of each and every one of you, and I am, too.

Onward. 🇺🇸

text:
My election observations... I'm titling it... "The Rope-a-Dope"... 

Trump is leaning against the ropes, congratulating the people throwing punches at him, while an entirely different fight unfolds around the ring...

Three days before the midterms, Trump posted Muhammad Ali's 1971 defeat against Joe Frazier... that caught my attention because Ali's greatest strategic masterpiece came three years later against George Foreman... the rope-a-dope...

Ali absorbed punishment against the ropes, allowing Foreman to exhaust himself while the crowd watched what appeared to be a losing fighter... then, in the eighth round, Ali came off those ropes and knocked Foreman out...

Now look at November 3... Dems capture Congress, the media celebrates, and Trump congratulates his opponents, praises their performance, and offers cooperation...

He distances himself from the losses, reminding everyone he wasn't on the ballot and still possesses presidential veto authority...

See the positioning? He's absorbing the blows while his opponents inherit responsibility for what follows...

Meanwhile another sequence was unfolding... in September, DOJ issued litigation holds covering election records in 29 states and Washington, D.C. On October 26, Trump announced a proposed $1 million election fraud reward, alongside DOJ's separate $10,000 to $30,000 fraud incentive program...

On October 29, DOJ reinforced the 22-month federal election record preservation requirement, warning against deliberate destruction... 

Then just one day before the election, a Michigan judge permanently blocked deletion of original electronic pollbooks after certification, preserving underlying data and metadata... "watch Michigan"...

Election evidence was being legally protected before the outcome was known...

Simultaneously ~1,000 DOJ monitors and observers covered 126 jurisdictions across all 50 states...

Hegseth mobilized military intelligence, Cyber Command, and the NSA against foreign interference, while DOJ's voter registration litigation tested federal authority against state sovereignty and privacy protections...

Election Day produced localized scanner failures, ballot shortages, bomb threats, and disruptions. Federal cyber monitoring reported limited threats and no identified foreign influence operations by late election night... preserved records now provide a foundation for lawful audits and investigations...

Zoom out and connect the systems... federal monitoring expanded as courts enforced constitutional boundaries... cyber defenses operated alongside evidence preservation... Congressional power shifted while the presidency retained its executive authority... and Trump is congratulating the Democrats...

Ali understood this dynamic... Foreman's aggression, confidence, and energy expenditure became variables influencing the fight... the punches were landing while conditions for Ali's counterattack developed...

Trump's Ali posts, his election response, and the institutional activity surrounding November 3 create a striking parallel...

The congressional defeat is real, legal processes continue, election records remain preserved, and Trump retains his constitutional powers...

Trump has absorbed the immediate political damage while positioning himself for the next phase...

The Democrats have their victory, the spotlight, and the illusion of victory... Trump is about to move off the ropes and come out swinging...

text:
🇺🇲 🇷🇺 Trump's Russian diesel deal is unraveling at sea.

A plan negotiated with Vladimir Putin to ease America's fuel crisis is running into legal resistance, reluctant buyers and tankers changing course. The Financial Times reports that two of the first three vessels initially heading toward the United States have diverted, while a third still lacks a confirmed unloading port.

One tanker, the Leruo, is now signaling Brazil as its destination. Another, the Talisman, has entered the Mediterranean and is awaiting orders. The Agioi Fanendes remains bound for the New York area, but its final discharge port has not been confirmed.

The reversal comes at a particularly difficult moment for Washington. U.S. diesel inventories have fallen below 100 million barrels for the first time in more than two decades. Diesel futures have risen more than 60% since Trump launched the war against Iran, and retail prices are approaching $6.30 a gallon.

The October agreement was intended to bring Russian fuel back into global markets and provide relief before the midterm elections. Trump temporarily eased sanctions, while Moscow agreed to resume exports.

But the arrangement has encountered a problem that a presidential announcement alone cannot resolve: American companies must still be willing and legally able to handle the shipments.

Lawmakers from both parties have questioned whether the sanctions waiver can override the 2022 congressional ban on Russian energy imports. New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill has warned port operators against accepting the cargoes, while potential buyers face uncertainty over legal exposure and reputational consequences.

For traders, the risks are substantial. A cargo may be commercially attractive, but an uncertain regulatory environment can make the transaction difficult to finance, insure or complete.

Brazil offers an alternative destination. Since Western restrictions redirected Russian petroleum exports, Brazilian importers have become established buyers of Russian diesel. A tanker changing its declared destination toward Brazil, however, does not establish that a final sale has been completed.

The wider implications extend beyond the shipping industry. Washington sought to use Russian fuel to contain the economic consequences of a war with Iran, even as Moscow continues its war against Ukraine.

The result exposes a central limitation of the agreement: easing sanctions does not automatically restore commercial relationships, eliminate congressional opposition or secure buyers.

For now, Russian diesel is moving through international waters, but the American market it was supposed to supply remains difficult to access.

text:
Nov. 5, 1911, 115 years ago tomorrow: Cal Rodgers landed in Pasadena and finished the first airplane flight across the United States. He had already missed the prize deadline by 19 days, and he kept flying anyway.

Publisher William Randolph Hearst offered $50,000 for a coast-to-coast flight in 30 days. Rodgers left Sheepshead Bay, New York, on Sept. 17 in a Wright EX biplane named Vin Fiz, after his sponsor's grape soda. When the 30 days ran out, he had only reached Kansas City.

A rail car full of spare parts chased him west. Two days before the finish, an engine cylinder exploded at 4,000 feet and drove steel shards into his arm. He glided back, got the engine fixed, and took off again.

Final tally: 49 days, about 82 hours in the air, averaging 51.5 mph.

Would you have kept going after the prize was gone?

5. Nut Olave Your Face 📉 −3 (6–2)

The 6–0 start created a useful cushion. The current injury list explains why Nut may need every bit of it.

A 152.60–124.00 loss to Jalen became much more damaging when Lamar’s return lasted one offensive play. He injured his throwing thumb, needs surgery and is headed to IR, with a season-ending absence possible. Nut had been waiting for an elite quarterback to return. Now the roster has to plan around potentially losing him for the rest of the fantasy season.

Lawrence scored 19.4, while Murray’s 19.9 sat on the bench. That would ordinarily provide two usable options, but Murray is dealing with hamstring soreness and Minnesota plays Monday night. Nut needs a plan before Sunday’s games lock. Waiting for a late decision without a replacement could force a skill-position player into superflex or leave the lineup exposed. 

The running back losses are also significant. Harvey is on IR with a knee injury and cannot return before Week 13. Etienne and Benson remain unavailable, and injured Tyrone Tracy was released. Cook is carrying a large share of the usable backfield value. Perine’s 2.9 after being added as a free agent showed the difficulty of finding a meaningful replacement in this league’s waiver pool. 

That makes the receiver group more important. London’s 1.8 followed an in-game head evaluation, Amon-Ra scored 12.6, Pickens had 6.8, and LaPorta added 6.5. McBride’s 20.2 and Cook’s 18.1 were the dependable offensive contributions. Jacksonville’s defense scored 21, more than any individual offensive starter.

Olave returning from New Orleans’s bye improves the available lineup immediately. Nut can lean more heavily on receivers in the flex positions rather than trying to manufacture running back depth that is not currently there. London, Amon-Ra, Olave, Pickens and McBride remain a strong enough foundation to win.

The matchup with Chase presents a clear contrast. Nut still has star power, but Chase currently has more stable quarterback options and healthier alternatives across the lineup. Nut’s best route is for the top receivers and McBride to produce together while Lawrence and, if healthy, Murray avoid a major deficit at quarterback.

Jacksonville’s Thursday matchup against Fagnano offers an early defensive opportunity. It could help offset some of the projected offensive disadvantage, though relying on another 20-point defense score would be optimistic.

The dynasty outlook remains strong because the receiver and tight end core is intact. The immediate championship outlook is weaker because injuries have concentrated so much responsibility into fewer healthy starters.

Win and both teams are 7–2. Lose and a 6–0 start becomes 6–3, with the playoff race suddenly much closer behind him.

Most of the 1.7 million weren’t new voters.  They were mainly people who vote in some elections but skipped 2022.

Higher turnout, about 1.1 million:  Turnout rose from 46% to 51.6%.

More registered voters, about 0.6 million:  Registration grew by about 1.3 million.

Where turnout grew most:  Border counties and large urban counties, with Hispanic voters a major factor.

First-time voters:  Roughly 6–10% of early voters had no voting record, based on partial, unofficial counts.

Abbott’s flat total: Some of his past voters likely switched to Hinojosa, with new Republican-leaning voters offsetting them, but the data can’t confirm that yet.

Turnout was 51.6%, below 2018’s 53% and 2024’s 61.2%, so the 9.8 million ballots don’t suggest inflated voting.  A state citizenship check of more than 18 million registrations flagged only 2,724, while Abbott lost by about 700,000 votes.  The FBI and local officials denied a viral claim of 20,000 fraudulent ballots in a Houston warehouse, and a Potter County GOP lawsuit over machine vulnerabilities offered no proof of them.  Texas also requires paper-based audits that can test the machine counts, Abbott conceded on the math, and a Republican analyst attributed the outcome to Democratic gains across the state.  If real fraud exists, it should appear as mismatches between paper ballots and machine totals, or as more ballots than voter check-ins, and neither has been reported so far.

text:
Life. You need to know when to walk away, know when to run and when to hold steady.

On July 26, 1977, in a New Orleans hotel room, Robert Plant answered a phone call that would tear his life in two

He was twenty-eight years old, leading the most powerful band on the planet, living among private jets, packed stadiums, and seemingly limitless success. Then he heard the voice of his wife, Maureen. And in an instant, everything fell apart.

Karac, their five-year-old son, was dead. A stomach virus, swift and merciless. No warning, no chance to intervene. While Robert sang on the other side of the ocean, his "little mountain man" was gone.

The tour stopped immediately. Plant flew to England in a state of shock that no amount of fame could allay. He found his son in the quiet of the Midlands, surrounded by a grief beyond words. That day, he looked for his bandmates. John Bonham was there, as devastated as he was. Jimmy Page and John Paul Jones were not. They did not show up at the funeral. Years later, they would talk about "respecting space," but for Robert, it was an absence that left a deep scar.

Something inside him cracked. He returned to his farm, stopped drinking, stopped taking drugs, stopped living like a rock star. He said he didn't want to be in Led Zeppelin anymore, that he just wanted to be with his family. He even applied for a job at a teachers' college, ready to leave music forever.

The only one who managed to bring him back was Bonham. Not with pressure, but with friendship. He'd show up at the farm driving a limousine, wearing a chauffeur's hat to make him laugh, and take him out for a quiet drink. He'd remind him that they were friends first, and musicians second. So Robert agreed to give it one last try.
In Through the Out Door was born, an album marked by an undisguised pain. Inside was All My Love, the most intimate tribute Plant ever wrote for his son.

In 1980, they were about to go back on tour. But tragedy wasn't over. On September 24th, during rehearsals, Bonham began drinking like never before. Forty shots of vodka in twelve hours. The next morning, he was dead. He was thirty-two years old.

Led Zeppelin issued a brief, almost terse statement: without Bonham, they couldn't continue. And they kept their word. No farewell tour, no replacement, no nostalgic outing. The biggest band in the world simply stopped.

For the next forty years, promoters from half the planet offered Plant astronomical sums for a reunion. Hundreds of millions for a single tour. Each time, he refused. Fans accused him of selfishness, of stubbornness. But Plant knew something they didn't: the "Golden God" had died in 1977, along with Karac.

Since then, he has built a new musical life. He explored folk, bluegrass, North African rhythms, sang with Alison Krauss, lowered his voice, let go of the cry that had made him immortal. He said he could no longer be that man, because that man no longer existed.
His story overturns the common idea of strength. It's not about moving forward at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop, when to protect what remains of truth. Plant chose his humanity over legend, life over myth.

Today he's seventy-six. He still plays, still creates, tours small venues. But he's never looked back. And perhaps this is his greatest lesson: you can buy everything except the past. And sometimes the bravest thing is to let go of what made you famous to save what made you human.

• Earlier estimate: 150 MMT.\

• Rice export offers from India and Pakistan have increased $20/tonne since July.\

THE EL NIÑO FACTOR:

Historical data from AMIS show that El Niño years have been associated with an average global paddy production shortfall of approximately 9.6 MMT.

India, Pakistan, Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam, the Philippines and Malaysia are all exposed to weather-related production risks.

BMI has revised its 2026 average CBOT rice futures forecast from $12.90 to $14/cwt.

However, an important distinction: futures have rallied much more aggressively than physical export prices. BMI says the physical market has not yet experienced a comparable supply shock.

THE BIGGER RISK:

If El Niño strengthens further, South and Southeast Asian paddy production could face another round of stress.

Rice is particularly vulnerable because global production is heavily concentrated in regions where El Niño often brings reduced rainfall.

For India, this is especially important: a weaker rice crop, tighter export availability and rising global prices could reshape the entire Asian rice trade.

Weather will be the key variable to watch through Q1 2027.

Vietjet will launch new services linking Colombo and the Maldives with Hanoi, Vietnam’s capital, further enhancing air connectivity between Sri Lanka and Vietnam while opening up more opportunities for Sri Lankan travellers to explore the world through the airline’s extensive flight network.

The Colombo-Hanoi and Maldives-Hanoi routes, with the latter operated via Colombo, are scheduled to commence operations on 9 February 2027. Passengers from Sri Lanka can book Colombo-Maldives flights separately, offering greater flexibility for their travel plans.

Together, these new routes strengthen Vietjet’s presence in South Asia, complementing its existing Colombo-Ho Chi Minh City route, its upcoming Maldives-Ho Chi Minh City service via Colombo and its extensive network connecting Vietnam with India.

For Sri Lankan visitors arriving in Hanoi, Vietnam’s capital offers an unforgettable introduction to the country. A city where centuries-old heritage meets contemporary energy, Hanoi invites travellers to wander through the atmospheric streets of its Old Quarter, enjoy a leisurely stroll around Hoan Kiem Lake, discover the Temple of Literature and savour its celebrated cuisine. Beyond the capital, travellers can venture to the spectacular landscapes of Ha Long Bay, the majestic mountains of northern Vietnam and the region’s charming traditional villages.

As Vietjet continues to broaden its international network, the airline is bringing the world closer to Vietnam with convenient and affordable connections. A new Da Nang–Jakarta route, launching on December 20, 2026, will operate four round-trip flights per week, further strengthening connectivity across Southeast Asia. Vietjet has also recently launched long-haul services from Hanoi to Almaty, Kazakhstan, and Prague, Czech Republic, opening up new travel opportunities between Vietnam, Central Asia and Europe.

With more flights from Colombo, Sri Lanka travellers can look forward to experiencing the unique charm of Vietnam, discovering new cultures, and creating memorable journeys. Through Vietjet’s growing network, passengers can also enjoy convenient onward connections to a wide range of destinations across Asia, Australia and Europe, making Vietjet an ideal travel partner for exploring the region and beyond.

text:
Washington paid Albert Haynesworth about $35 million for 20 games and 6.5 sacks. He says the team lied to get him there.

In 2008 he was an All-Pro defensive tackle in Tennessee, playing on a one-year franchise tag worth $7.25 million.

He says he got his ask down to $32 million over four years. He says the Titans answered with $28 million.

Reports at the time put the Titans' final offer at four years and $34 million, with about $20 million guaranteed.

In February 2009 Washington gave him seven years and $100 million, with $41 million guaranteed. At the time it was the most guaranteed money in NFL history.

His agent woke him up with the call. His first reaction was that 41 was an ugly number and could they make it 45.

Then Mike Shanahan arrived in 2010 and moved the team to a 3-4 defense. Haynesworth had built his career as a 4-3 tackle.

He says he asked before signing if he would play the same defense he played in Tennessee, and was told yes.

Washington offered to release him if he did not take a $21 million bonus due April 1, 2010. He took the money.

Then he skipped offseason workouts, needed 10 days to pass a conditioning test, and was suspended without pay for the last four games of 2010.

In July 2011 Washington traded him to New England for a fifth-round pick.

The case for Haynesworth:
He signed to play one system and the team changed it after he signed.
Washington offered the money. Nobody forced them to guarantee $41 million.
Tennessee had him on a one-year tag and would not come close to his ask.

The case for Washington:
They paid him about $35 million and got 6.5 sacks.
He took the $21 million bonus, then refused to do what the coaches asked.
A contract pays you to play the position the coach gives you.

Is it fair that Haynesworth kept $35 million from Washington?

text:
About one in three Australian babies labelled with a peanut allergy may not have one after all.

A national evaluation of the ADAPT Peanut Oral Immunotherapy Program, led by Murdoch Children's Research Institute and the National Allergy Centre of Excellence, assessed 1,275 infants across 10 paediatric public hospitals in Victoria, New South Wales, Queensland, South Australia and Western Australia. Of the 778 who sat a supervised oral food challenge, 34.8% had no reaction. Those infants could have the allergy label removed and keep peanut in their diet in an age-appropriate form, such as peanut butter.

The remaining 65.2% did react, including anaphylaxis in 12% of positive challenges (7.8% of all challenges). Every episode was managed safely by the hospital teams. Among 394 infants who then started oral immunotherapy at a dose guided by the challenge, 97.5% successfully began treatment.

Skin prick tests and Ara h 2 blood levels were higher on average in babies who reacted, but they did not predict the dose that triggered a reaction or how severe it would be. History and allergy tests alone were not enough.

ADAPT, launched in 2024, is the first peanut allergy treatment program offered in Australian public hospitals for infants outside a clinical trial. The study, published in The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology: In Practice, concludes that a supervised oral food challenge should be routinely considered to confirm peanut allergy in infants before immunotherapy or avoidance.

What on earth are we doing?

​Yes, we need strong, secure borders. Yes, we need to fix the madness around Net Zero. 

But if we don’t fix the core fundamentals of daily life for regular people, the entire system is going to crumble.

​Right now, the basic work-life contract in this country is broken. 

The fundamental equation that underpins a stable society MUST be:
​WORK = HOUSE = FAMILY = SECURITY = OPPORTUNITY
​If a full-time job doesn't guarantee you a home, stability, and a future to pass on to your kids, then the government is failing at its most basic job.

​We don't need endless political infighting or cheap scapegoating of welfare. We need radical action on the two biggest cost drivers crushing workers and businesses: HOUSING and ENERGY.

​Here is how we fix it:

​🏡 1. Slash House Prices to 3x Average Earnings
Bring house prices back to a realistic ratio so working people can actually buy a home, build equity, and start families instead of paying off someone else's mortgage in high rents forever.

​⚡ 2. Slash Energy Bills in Half with Bold UK Tech
We have world-class technology right here in the UK with Rolls-Royce Small Modular Reactors (SMRs). Let's cut the bureaucratic red tape:
​Offer SMR deployments directly to energy-hungry industries, manufacturing plants, and logistics hubs.

​In return for streamlined permissions or co-funding, any excess energy generated flows straight into the national grid for free.

​Double down on cheap, reliable, base-load power to cut household and business energy bills by 50%.
​If house prices and energy bills were cut in half tomorrow, the debate over welfare overspend and high taxes would vanish overnight. 

People would have disposable income, businesses could afford to invest and pay better wages, and the economy would boom naturally.

​Stop letting politicians split us into boxes—welfare vs. workers, workers vs. businesses. We need ALL of us on the same side demanding a system that puts native Brits and working families first.

​Demand government fulfill the work contract. It’s time to wake up and rebuild the fundamentals.

To everyone on the right of politics: It’s time to stop letting politicians split us into competing camps—

welfare recipients, low-paid workers, middle-class earners, and business owners. We need to bring all of these groups together under one roof.

​It’s time to start holding right-wing politicians to account. 

Demand that they stop hiding behind standard lines about tax cuts for corporations while ignoring the crushing burden on regular families. 

Putting the country first means putting everybody first—workers, families, the vulnerable, and businesses alike.
​If the right cannot deliver a decent, secure, and affordable quality of life for its own people, then it has no purpose. 

Stop following blindly. Demand better, demand unity, and make them put the people first.
